title: Contextualized Graph Embeddings via Dynamic Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that addresses the limitations of existing techniques in capturing dynamic and contextual relationships within graphs. Traditional graph embedding methods often treat graphs as static structures, failing to account for the evolving nature of connections and the influence of temporal factors. We propose a framework leveraging Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to model the probabilistic dependencies between nodes and their attributes over time. The resulting contextualized graph embeddings effectively represent temporal influences and evolving connections, providing a richer and more accurate representation of graph data. The core innovation lies in integrating graph embedding techniques with the dynamic modeling capabilities of DBNs, resulting in a system capable of producing embeddings that are sensitive to both the structural and temporal aspects of the graph. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a theoretical framework and discuss its potential applications in various domains where dynamic graph analysis is crucial.

title: Quantum Teleportation-Based Distributed Data Transmission Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel protocol for secure distributed data transmission leveraging the principles of quantum teleportation. The core claim of this protocol is to achieve secure data transmission utilizing quantum teleportation technology. The proposed mechanism relies on quantum entanglement to facilitate the instantaneous transfer of quantum states and incorporates classical communication for error correction, thereby ensuring both the security and reliability of the transmission process. The significance of this work lies in its potential to provide a higher level of security compared to traditional data transmission methods. The protocol details the necessary steps, including entanglement distribution, state transfer, and classical communication phases, with a focus on minimizing the impact of noise and maintaining the integrity of the transmitted information. This protocol offers a viable pathway for building quantum networks capable of secure data exchange, contributing to advancements in quantum cryptography and distributed quantum computing.

title: 基于多尺度时空域的视频异常检测
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to video anomaly detection based on multi-scale spatiotemporal feature learning. Traditional video anomaly detection methods often struggle with the inherent complexities of capturing both local and global context within video sequences, leading to limited accuracy and robustness. Our approach addresses this limitation by leveraging the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to extract features from different scales and temporal dimensions. Specifically, we construct a multi-scale model that fuses spatial and temporal information effectively. The core claim of this research is that utilizing video features at different scales and across time will improve anomaly detection precision and robustness. The core mechanism involves combining CNNs for local feature extraction and RNNs for global temporal context understanding, followed by a multi-scale fusion process for robust anomaly identification. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in identifying anomalies in various video datasets.

title: Contextual Graph Neural Networks with Episodic Memory
abstract: This paper introduces Contextual Graph Neural Networks (CGNNs) with Episodic Memory, a novel approach to graph representation learning that addresses the limitations of standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in handling contextual information across multiple graph instances. The core claim is that conventional GNNs struggle to retain and effectively utilize contextual knowledge, leading to suboptimal performance when dealing with sequential graph data. To overcome this, we integrate an episodic memory module into a GNN architecture. This module enables the network to store and retrieve relevant information from past interactions, fostering more robust and transferable graph representations. The proposed framework provides a mechanism for learning from sequences of graphs, enhancing the network's ability to capture complex dependencies and patterns. Experiments (simulated) demonstrate the superior performance of CGNNs compared to traditional GNNs in scenarios requiring contextual understanding. We outline the key components, the integration process, and potential future research directions.

title: 多体量子态的自适应映射
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework based on adaptive mapping of multi-particle quantum states. The framework aims to extract specific features from high-dimensional quantum states and dynamically map these states, offering enhanced control and adaptability compared to traditional quantum algorithms. The core mechanism leverages quantum state self-adaptation to identify and manipulate key characteristics of the states. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the framework's efficacy in extracting specific features from complex quantum states and performing automated adjustments. This work represents a significant step toward dynamic quantum state manipulation, opening up new possibilities for quantum algorithm design and exploration.

title: Probability Logic Networks: Adaptive Learning Algorithm
abstract: Probability Logic Networks (GLP) represent a novel approach to modeling complex systems by leveraging probabilistic reasoning and learning. This paper introduces a new adaptive learning algorithm for GLP, designed to improve model performance on specific datasets through self-adaptation of key parameters. The core mechanism centers around a dynamically adjusted parameter learning process, enabling the network to refine its internal representations and achieve superior generalization capabilities. This work addresses a critical limitation of traditional GLP approaches – their lack of adaptability – offering a potentially transformative improvement in model performance.

title: Quantum-Adaptive Topology Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Quantum-Adaptive Topology Algorithm (QAT) designed to address complex topology problems. The algorithm leverages quantum self-adaptation to dynamically adjust the topology of a problem, offering improved performance compared to traditional approaches. We propose a mechanism that utilizes quantum states to iteratively refine a topological structure, enabling automated optimization and efficient solution of intricate problems. The core of this algorithm lies in the application of quantum self-correction, allowing for a flexible and adaptable topology formation. This approach has the potential to significantly advance the field of topology by providing a powerful tool for automated solution and optimization.

title: Predicting Your Own Failure Is Not Predicting Another Model's Advantage: What Router Results Establish About Agent Self-Knowledge, and the Incremental-Validity Test Nobody Has Run
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. A common reading of the LLM routing literature holds that delegation works without self-knowledge: a router allocates queries using external features of the task and observed outcome statistics over a model pool, and never consults the candidate model's opinion of its own competence. This paper argues that the reading does not survive the evidence. Signals derived from the candidate model's own generation are competitive with trained external routers and, in the one located comparison that varies distribution shift, substantially better out of distribution; a self-confidence gate has been reported to beat a frozen external router at lower token cost; and the strongest current cascade and escalation systems are built on exactly such signals. What the evidence does support is a different partition, which the internal-versus-external frame obscures. Predicting whether you will fail is a self-directed prediction and is comparatively tractable. Predicting which alternative would do better is an other-directed prediction, and the same score that ranks own-failure well has been reported to fall sharply when asked which collaboration protocol pays off. Delegation is the second kind of judgement, not the first, and the learning-to-defer literature has known for years that a deferral rule must model the expert rather than only the deferrer. A further problem is that no located routing experiment isolates introspection at all. Every deployed self-signal is a supervised probe fitted to labelled outcomes, which is an external estimator that happens to read internal features, so the axis the delegation story rests on is not the axis the experiments vary. The control that would settle it already exists in the introspection literature, where a model's self-prediction is scored against what a second model with matched knowledge predicts about it. That control has not been run on a router. Four measurements are set out that would settle the open part, and what is not known is stated flatly: nobody has reported whether self-assessed capability adds anything to a delegation decision once an external estimator with the same information is already in the system. The literature search, drafting and citation verification for this paper were carried out with AI assistance under the author's direction. Every citation was machine-verified against the arXiv API and Crossref before inclusion, and every quantitative claim was read back against the cited source's own abstract. The author is responsible for the final text and for all claims made in it.

title: Machine learning-assisted calibration of Agent-based Models: surrogate-based optimization with Genetic Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization
abstract: Calibrating an agent-based model (ABM) is difficult because its objective landscape is stochastic and rugged, and can be evaluated only through costly black-box simulations. This study adapts inner-loop surrogate-assisted evolutionary computation (SAEC) to ABM calibration by embedding a machine-learning surrogate within genetic algorithm (GA) and particle swarm optimisation (PSO). At each iteration, the surrogate screens the candidates and the simulator validates only the top 50%, reducing simulation demand while correcting surrogate errors. We evaluate a full factorial of 48 configurations combining two optimisers, five surrogates, and four calibration objectives on two contrasting ABMs, the Brock-Hommes asset-pricing model and the Island growth model. Parameter recovery is measured against pseudo-true values. Relative to the strongest pure-optimiser baseline, the best ML-assisted configurations reduce RMSE by 20.0% on Brock-Hommes and 63.8% on Island, while reducing computation time by 32.1% and 61.1%, respectively. ANOVA with Dunnett's post-hoc tests confirms significant time savings for every surrogate under both Brock-Hommes optimisers and under GA on Island. No surrogate differs significantly from the pure-optimiser baseline in parameter-recovery accuracy on Island; the reported accuracy gains are therefore best-configuration outcomes rather than average effects resolved at this sample size. The best surrogate-optimiser-objective combination changes with ABM complexity, indicating that surrogate-assisted calibration depends on the model and does not admit a universal default recipe.

title: WolfSociety: Understanding Collective Risk from Harmful-Agent Scaling in Financial Agent Societies
abstract: Safety evaluations typically focus on individual agents, but interacting agents can spread harmful information and influence the environment in which later decisions are made. We study how collective failure changes with harmful-agent fraction and society size in a controlled financial agent society, where agents communicate over a social network and trade in a shared market. In the primary financial scenario, collective failure requires broad harmful diffusion together with severe price dislocation or liquidity stress. Across all tested society sizes, failure remains rare at low harmful fractions but rises sharply over a narrow range. As society size grows from N=100 to N=2000, the harmful fraction associated with a 50% failure probability decreases from 4.7% to 2.2%, while the corresponding number of harmful agents increases from approximately 5 to 44. In contrast, when the number of harmful agents is held fixed, their impact becomes weaker as the society grows. Controlled interventions further show that broader network reach shifts the collapse boundary toward lower harmful fractions, whereas stronger conformity alone has little effect. To characterize these effects, we introduce Agent Society Dynamics, a finite-size framework for relating harmful-agent fraction, society size, and interaction structure to collective failure. Overall, our results reveal a nonlinear, size-dependent collapse transition in financial agent societies, showing that collective failure depends not only on the prevalence of harmful agents but also on the size and interaction structure of the surrounding society. Code is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/WolfSociety.

title: Coupled Control and Wireless World Models for Resilient Remote Robotic Control
abstract: Remote robotic systems operating over wireless networks must maintain reliable control despite limited communication resources, changing channel conditions, and environmental disturbances.However, continuously transmitting high-dimensional sensory observations, such as camera images, increases communication overhead and energy consumption while reducing robustness under unreliable connectivity.To address these challenges, this paper proposes a resilient communication-aware remote robotic control framework based on coupled control and wireless Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models that jointly capture robot dynamics and wireless channel evolution from visual observations and a combination of raw and structured radio frequency (RF) representations based on spectrograms and Persistence Images(PIs).The learned latent representations enable predictive communication scheduling by jointly forecasting future robot states and wireless conditions, thereby reducing unnecessary uplink transmissions while maintaining reliable control performance.Furthermore, an adaptive resilience mechanism detects latent prediction discrepancies and efficiently adapts perception embeddings to accommodate wireless and visual environmental changes without retraining the complete control policy.The proposed framework is evaluated in a synchronized Gazebo-Robot Operating System (ROS)-Sionna robot-wireless simulation environment under diverse wireless propagation and perception perturbations.Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in communication efficiency, robustness, and resilience while maintaining navigation performance compared with conventional Proportional Integral Derivative (PID), model-free Deep Q-Network (DQN), and predictive approaches based on Vision Transformers(ViTs).

title: The Language of Chatbots as a Tool for Building Customer Satisfaction in Digital Marketing
abstract: This project focuses on the language of chatbots as a tool for building customer satisfaction in digital marketing. It addresses the growing use of chatbots in digital brand communication and the need for systematic research into their linguistic, stylistic and pragmatic strategies in the Slovak e-commerce environment. The research examines how chatbot language influences customer experience, trust, satisfaction, brand perception and willingness to continue interaction. It combines corpus-linguistic, qualitative, quantitative and experimental approaches, including the analysis of real chatbot interactions and the testing of linguistic variants. The project aims to develop an interdisciplinary framework for evaluating the quality of chatbot communication and to formulate practical recommendations for linguistically and marketing-effective chatbots. This OSF page serves as a transparent archive of selected project outputs, publications, conference materials, datasets and supplementary research documentation.

title: Title: Non-Local Constraint Propagation via Quantum Entanglement
abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a fundamentally new approach to constraint propagation, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical methods. This paper explores the implementation of a mechanism for efficiently transmitting and adapting constraints across quantum systems, leveraging entanglement to detect inconsistencies and dynamically adjust constraints in real-time. The core claim is that this approach can revolutionize complex system modeling by enabling a more efficient and robust form of constraint propagation. We detail the theoretical framework, the architecture of the entanglement-based constraint propagation system, and the initial experimental results demonstrating its potential. This work addresses the challenge of maintaining constraint consistency in large-scale quantum systems while minimizing communication overhead. The focus is on a novel method of leveraging entanglement for verifiable constraint refinement, ultimately offering a paradigm shift in the handling of complex quantum models.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a unique paradigm for information encoding, potentially enabling novel computational paradigms. This paper investigates the application of quantum entanglement to an adaptive optimization algorithm, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional optimization methods in complex problem domains. We propose a novel approach leveraging the inherent properties of entangled states to dynamically adjust optimization parameters, thereby facilitating the discovery of global optima. The core mechanism centers around the manipulation of entangled states to guide the search process, leading to improved performance. The significance of this research lies in exploring a potential paradigm shift in optimization, driven by the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

title: Title: Topology-Based Cryptography with Dynamic Structure
abstract: This paper explores the potential of topology as a foundation for cryptographic systems, focusing on a novel approach that dynamically constructs a mathematical topology based on input data. The core claim is that this system, leveraging the inherent complexity of the data, provides unbreakable encryption through a structure that is inherently difficult to analyze, rendering traditional cryptanalysis ineffective. We present a theoretical framework and initial design for such a system, outlining the key components – the evolving topology, data integration, and security analysis – and discussing potential challenges and future research directions. The study emphasizes the unique properties of topology, specifically its ability to represent and manipulate complex relationships, and how this can be exploited for robust cryptographic applications.

title: Information-Driven Quantum Entanglement Distribution
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum entanglement distribution, aiming to overcome limitations imposed by classical communication delays and the inherent fragility of entanglement. We propose a protocol centered around a "resonance" mechanism – a subtle and non-local adjustment – that stabilizes entanglement across vast distances, significantly reducing decoherence. The core claim is that this method, leveraging this resonance phenomenon, can achieve entanglement distribution with substantially enhanced robustness and scalability. We detail the proposed protocol, its mathematical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness. The research focuses on mitigating the detrimental effects of decoherence through a carefully crafted entanglement state manipulation, ultimately offering a potentially transformative approach to quantum information transfer.

title: 基于图的自然语言处理的语义关系建模
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to semantic relation modeling in Natural Language Processing (NLP) utilizing graph-based representations. The core principle is to model lexical relationships as a graph, where nodes represent words and edges represent semantic connections. We propose a self-adaptive graph structure optimization algorithm to dynamically adjust the graph's structure based on the input text, enabling a more nuanced and robust understanding of word relationships. The implementation demonstrates improved performance on several benchmark datasets, validating the proposed method's effectiveness in capturing subtle semantic nuances. The core mechanism leverages graph theory principles to enhance semantic comprehension, offering a significant advancement over traditional vector-based approaches.

title: Title: Computational Complexity for Algorithmic Design
abstract: The pursuit of efficient algorithms is fundamental to technological progress. However, traditional approaches often rely on static complexity metrics, failing to capture the nuanced dynamics of algorithm design. This paper introduces a novel computational framework leveraging evolutionary algorithms and simulated annealing to automatically design and optimize complex algorithmic designs, moving beyond simple complexity assessments. We propose a system that actively shapes the design process through iterative refinement, incorporating features directly impacting performance and scalability. This work addresses a critical gap in the field by providing a more dynamic and adaptive approach to algorithm design, offering a potential pathway towards significantly enhanced computational performance. The core mechanism involves employing evolutionary algorithms to explore a vast design space, guided by simulated annealing to minimize performance degradation and improve scalability. This framework aims to represent a fundamental shift towards a more intelligent and automated design process, reducing the need for manual intervention and facilitating the discovery of novel algorithmic solutions.

title: Quantum Chaos: Harnessing Chaos Control to Mitigate Decoherence in Quantum Systems
abstract: Decoherence, the process by which quantum systems lose their quantum properties due to interaction with the environment, poses a significant challenge to the development and application of quantum information processing. This work explores a novel approach to mitigating decoherence by leveraging principles from chaos theory – specifically, chaos control. We investigate how controlled chaotic dynamics can be employed to effectively counteract the detrimental effects of decoherence, ultimately aiming to prolong the coherence time of quantum states. The core idea is to introduce carefully designed external drives that induce chaotic behavior within the quantum system, effectively 'smearing out' the decoherence process. This approach contrasts with traditional methods, which often focus on isolating the quantum system from its environment. We present a theoretical framework for analyzing this interaction, utilizing concepts such as Lyapunov exponents and phase space reconstruction to characterize the chaotic dynamics and quantify the impact on decoherence. Our results suggest a promising new avenue for quantum information protection, potentially leading to more robust and efficient quantum computing and communication technologies. We define key parameters such as the initial state of the system (s_0), the external driving force (F), the system Hamiltonian (H), and the decoherence rate (γ). The effectiveness of this approach is quantified through the evolution of the quantum state, represented by the time-dependent probability amplitudes (ψ(t)).

title: Formal Verification of Secure Multi-Party Computation Protocols
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) allows multiple parties to compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. However, ensuring the security and correctness of MPC protocols is a notoriously difficult task, largely due to the complexity involved in modeling and analyzing potential attacks. This paper presents a novel approach to formally verifying MPC protocols using zero-knowledge proof systems. The core of our method lies in translating the protocol's logic into a verifiable system, enabling rigorous proof of security against a defined set of attacks. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and highlight its potential for significantly enhancing the trustworthiness of MPC implementations. The focus is on providing a systematic method for assessing the robustness of protocols and reducing the reliance on informal security arguments. This work contributes to a more secure and reliable future for distributed computing.

title: Title: Quantum State Representation as a Symbolic Language
abstract: Quantum state representation is a fundamental challenge in quantum information theory, demanding a robust and expressive language to model the complexities of quantum mechanics. This paper explores the development of a novel symbolic language, "Quantum State Representation," designed to address these challenges by explicitly incorporating key quantum concepts such as entanglement, superposition, and coherence. We propose a formal grammar based on principles derived from quantum information theory, aiming to facilitate more efficient analysis, manipulation, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of quantum systems. The core claim is that this new language offers a significant advancement over existing methods, providing enhanced conceptual clarity and computational efficiency.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entropy Decoupling (DQA) - Dynamic Topology Parameter Adjustment
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic quantum entropy decoupling (DQA) algorithm designed to optimize quantum system performance by dynamically adjusting entropy parameters. Traditional quantum error correction relies on pre-determined, fixed entropy levels, which often struggle to adapt to evolving system states. The DQA algorithm dynamically adjusts these parameters based on input data, enabling a more flexible and responsive approach to quantum system optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential to surpass existing error correction methods in specific scenarios. The core mechanism involves a continuous feedback loop that adapts the entropy distribution based on measured data, leading to improved fidelity and reduced noise.

title: Square-Root Fibers and Complement Codes Modulo 144
abstract: Square-Root Fibers and Complement Codes Modulo 144 develops a compact finite-algebra classification inside the multiplicative unit group modulo 144. The paper begins with the congruence x squared equals 25 modulo 144 and determines its eight unit solutions. Each solution has multiplicative order 12, and pairing the roots by the unique order-two element produces exactly four cyclic subgroups of order 12. These four subgroups share the same six-state square subgroup, giving a complete classification of the relevant cyclic order-12 structures through a single square-root equation. For a distinguished cyclic order-12 subgroup, the fourth-power map divides the twelve group elements into three canonical fibers of four elements each. Taking the complements of these three fibers produces three eight-element incidence vectors satisfying a binary parity relation. The paper then generalizes this construction. For any set partitioned into three equal parts of size m, the complements of those parts generate a binary linear code of length 3m, dimension 2, and minimum distance 2m. The modulo-144 construction therefore gives a concrete binary code with parameters [12,2,8]. A geometric interpretation is also developed: the four cyclic order-12 subgroups appear as pairs of regular hexagons sharing a common six-state square spine, with four possible relative angular offsets. All results are finite and exact. The paper is independent of any broader physical, archaeological, or interpretive framework. Literature novelty for the elementary group-theoretic and coding-theoretic components is not claimed pending a dedicated comparison with existing results.

title: Five safes task execution service: a standards-based architecture and reference implementation for secure federated analytics across trusted research environments
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Design, implement, and evaluate a standards-based architecture for secure federated analytics across heterogeneous Trusted Research Environments (TREs) that aligns with the Five Safes Framework, without requiring TREs to modify their internal governance, infrastructure, or operational practices. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The Five Safes task execution service (TES) architecture standardizes the format of analysis requests and handles analysis execution and release of outputs consistent with the Five Safes Framework. The Global Alliance for Genomics and Health TES standard is used for submitting analyses to TREs. Three logical layers support federated analytics: a Submission and Orchestration Layer outside the TRE accepts analyses and holds outputs for collection; a Controller Layer inside the TRE enforces local governance policies and manages disclosure control; and an Analysis Execution Layer governs the technical execution of approved analytics against sensitive data. An open-source reference implementation was developed and deployed in 2 real-world case studies. RESULTS: Five Safes TES was deployed to enable federated analytics within the Dementias Platform UK national research infrastructure. In a transcontinental deployment, federated analytics across 2 TREs hosted in Singapore was enabled by Submission and Orchestration Layers hosted in the United Kingdom, demonstrating multi-jurisdictional federated analytics without centralizing control or moving sensitive data. DISCUSSION: By aligning open technical standards with established governance frameworks, the architecture supports heterogeneous TREs participating in federated analyses while preserving data sovereignty, institutional autonomy, and compliance with local governance requirements. CONCLUSION: Five Safes TES demonstrates how TRE federated analytics can be deployed as a routine research capability, rather than requiring bespoke technical development.

title: A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction
abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

title: Moments of crosscorrelation demerit factors of binary sequences
abstract: Families of sequences with low mutual aperiodic crosscorrelation assist the design of systems for multi-user asynchronous communications and multiple-input multiple-output radar. The crosscorrelation demerit factor of a pair of sequences is the sum of the squared magnitudes of their crosscorrelation values at every shift when the sequences are normalized to unit Euclidean norm, and the merit factor is the reciprocal of the demerit factor. For each positive integer $\ell$, we endow the $2^{2 \ell}$ pairs of binary sequences of length $\ell$ with uniform probability measure and study the distribution of their crosscorrelation demerit factors. Sarwate showed that the mean value is always $1$ regardless of length $\ell$. We develop a method for finding an exact formula for the $p$th central moment (for any positive integer $p$) as a function of $\ell$. Formulae for the variance and third central moment ($p=2$ and $3$) are then obtained by hand calculations, while the fourth through sixth central moments are obtained by computer-assisted calculations. Our theory also shows that all the central moments must be strictly positive for $p\geq 2$ and $\ell \geq 3$.

title: VoxelFix: Post-Hoc Semantic Correction of Completed 3D Voxel Maps
abstract: Semantic 3D maps are increasingly constructed automatically for aerial robotics by integrating learned semantic predictions into 3D representations. While this avoids costly manual 3D annotation, errors in the perception and mapping pipeline can persist in the resulting map, reducing its reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing 3D semantic map refinement methods either rely on the original observations, treat occupancy as part of the prediction problem, or apply non-learned local regularization to completed maps. Instead, we study post-hoc semantic correction, asking whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping its geometry and occupancy fixed. We introduce \method, a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To obtain training pairs, we corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. We evaluate \method on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models. \method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23--5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across the evaluated semantic classes and particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond the environments seen during training.

title: ElderBench: Benchmarking Autonomous Mobile Agents for Older Adults
abstract: While autonomous mobile agents hold great potential for assisting older adults with smartphone usage, existing GUI benchmarks mainly rely on explicit, goal-oriented instructions and rarely capture the naturally occurring language patterns of older users, such as indirect speech, referential ambiguity, and under-specified requests. This mismatch between benchmark instructions and real-world elderly interactions may hinder reliable agent deployment. To address this gap, we present ElderBench, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile GUI agents in authentic elderly-oriented scenarios. ElderBench is constructed from 249 naturally elicited smartphone tasks collected from older adults across 20 applications. We first characterize the linguistic divergence between elderly instructions and existing GUI benchmark instructions from syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic perspectives. We then evaluate mainstream GUI agents and Vision-Language Models under both online and offline settings, revealing substantial performance degradation when handling elderly-oriented instructions. Through controlled instruction normalization, failure analysis, and fine-grained linguistic feature analysis, we further identify how elderly-specific language patterns contribute to agent failures. Our findings provide actionable design insights toward more adaptive, interpretable, and age-inclusive GUI agents for older adults.

title: Användningen av artificiell intelligens i strategisk planering
abstract: This bachelor’s thesis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is used in strategic planning and what benefits, opportunities, challenges, and limitations are identified in existing research. Strategic planning is examined through three components: goal articulation, strategy formulation, and resource allocation. The study was conducted as a structured literature review. The findings show that AI currently supports individual planning tasks rather than managing the strategic planning process. In goal articulation, personalized feedback from large language models can help users formulate more specific goals and implementation intentions. AI-related methods can also support the assessment of performance indicators connected to existing objectives. In strategy formulation, AI can generate and evaluate strategic alternatives, organize information, and support scenario analysis. In resource allocation, machine-learning models are mainly used to screen investment opportunities and research projects. The evidence suggests that AI is most useful when a task involves processing existing information, comparing alternatives, or making predictions. Its contribution becomes more limited when decisions require agreement on values, acceptance of uncertainty, or responsibility for long-term consequences. The main challenges include inconsistent outputs, dependence on historical data, limited explainability, confidentiality concerns, and unclear accountability. The available evidence is also uneven: research on organizational goal articulation remains limited, while resource-allocation studies mainly concern venture capital and research funding. The thesis concludes that AI can broaden and strengthen the analysis supporting strategic planning, but it should not be treated as an independent strategic authority. Managers remain responsible for evaluating its outputs and making final decisions.

title: The Authorship Dilemma: Navigating Copyright Ownership in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: Copyright law rests on the premise that a protected work originates in the intellectual labour of an identifiable human author, and it allocates ownership, economic rights and control by reference to that authorship. Generative artificial intelligence unsettles that premise by producing expressive work through algorithmic processes in which the human contribution may be confined to a prompt, a selection among outputs or a subsequent refinement. This article examines the resulting dilemma. It shows that the traditional doctrines of originality, human authorship, the idea and expression dichotomy, ownership, work made for hire, joint authorship and derivative works yield inconsistent or indeterminate results when applied to machine-generated material, and that the difficulty is one of incompatibility rather than of interpretation. It maps the possible claimants to authorship, being the user, the developer, the platform owner and the contributors of training data, and finds that none satisfies the classical test, so that the public domain becomes a plausible default. It compares the positions taken in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, India, China and Australia, and considers the philosophical theories of personality, labour and utility. It concludes that the answer lies not in deciding whether a machine can be an author but in reforming copyright to separate authorship, creative contribution and ownership, and proposes a tiered framework calibrated to the degree of human creative control.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian Federated Learning for Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation at the Edge
abstract: Edge translation systems must balance limited computation, data locality, and weak performance on low-resource language pairs. This study presents Multitask Bayesian Federated Learning (MT-BayesFL), a multilingual translation framework that combines a lightweight shared encoder, task-specific decoders, matrix-normal posteriors over shared attention projections, and covariance-aware server aggregation.

abstract: On 2026-08-14 I published an article on the Google Security blog with an update on HEIR, our homomorphic encryption (HE) compiler. This is a companion article, in which I have no limits on word count or jargon, and I can feel free to be honest. So strap in. title: OpenLogic in Marathi (mr-Deva-IN): Eight Chapters — v0.6, 65 of 722 source units
abstract: Corrective successor to seven-chapters-v0.5. The earlier reader exposed the frozen upstream Git revision in its front matter. This version replaces that raw identifier in the PDF, assembled TeX, and offline HTML with a short Marathi pointer to the project records. The exact source identity remains in the technical README, release manifest, and provenance. The immutable v0.5 record is preserved. Translation scope is unchanged: 59 of 722 source units, OLP-0004–OLP-0062; 663 units remain unfinished. The partial Marathi edition contains seven complete chapters of The Open Logic Text: Sets, Relations, Functions, Size of Sets, Arithmetization, Infinite Sets, and Syntax and Semantics in propositional logic. It includes 716 aligned content segments and 51 reader sections. Files include an 83-page PDF; offline HTML with local fonts, 3,373 native MathML expressions, thirteen figures with detailed Marathi alternatives, linked contents and keyboard-focusable formula regions; an assembled TeX reader; editable aligned Marathi TeX and pristine frozen English; a shared-schema expert-review bundle with 187 applied decisions and 4,474 exact current occurrences; a release manifest; and SHA-256 checksums. A byte-level TeX comparison confirms one intended front-matter line replacement. Render comparison confines the PDF change to page 1; pages 2–83 are pixel-identical to v0.5. Two clean guarded two-pass builds yielded identical PDF bytes on the same host. The changed page passed visual review. Exact HTML checks and Chromium review at 1280×720 and 390×844 passed with all thirteen figures loaded, 204 valid internal links, no page-level horizontal overflow, and keyboard scrolling of the widest mobile formula. Canonical decision JSON and working/release package consistency checks passed. Codex produced the machine translation and same-agent bilingual review. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed; specialist choices remain reversible. Assistive-technology behavior and cross-platform byte identity are not independently certified. Native scholarly canon originals are research evidence and are not redistributed. The Open Logic Project is credited as creator of the original text and does not endorse this translation. The text and marked adaptation use CC BY 4.0; inherited component notices and the SIL Open Font License remain in the editable package. This record is a new version in the existing Marathi OpenLogic DOI lineage.

title: Nonlinear Quantum Geometry: Adaptive Topology Structures
abstract: This paper explores the potential of nonlinear quantum geometry as a foundation for novel quantum computing architectures. We propose a model based on quantum entanglement, introducing a "quantum entanglement topology" mechanism to dynamically adjust the topology of quantum systems. This model offers a radical departure from traditional approaches by leveraging the inherent properties of entanglement, enabling the creation of complex, self-organized quantum states. The core claim is that this framework can facilitate the construction of robust and scalable quantum computers, particularly through the implementation of a fundamental layer for quantum computation. This work investigates the mathematical properties and potential applications of this proposed methodology, highlighting its unique capabilities and potential for advancing quantum information processing.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum State Encoding and Expansion
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of self-adaptive quantum state encoding and expansion techniques to significantly enhance quantum computation. The core focus is on leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum information theory to dynamically modify and expand quantum states, addressing limitations of traditional approaches. We propose a novel method that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to optimize performance and explore new computational pathways. The paper details the underlying principles, introduces a key mechanism for state modification, and outlines the potential benefits of this approach. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical and potential practical implications is presented. The research aims to contribute to the advancement of quantum computing by providing a framework for more versatile and powerful quantum systems.

title: Nonlinear Geometry Topology Structure Research
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental theoretical basis of quantum entanglement through the application of non-linear geometry topology. We explore a model based on non-Euclidean geometry, constructing a quantum entanglement framework that leverages its inherent non-linear properties. A novel quantum information processing algorithm is proposed, based on this model, aiming to simulate quantum entanglement with enhanced computational capabilities. The study aims to challenge existing quantum entanglement theories, which are primarily rooted in classical geometry, and potentially unveil new approaches to quantum information processing.

title: Core Claim: A Self-Adaptive Topological Quantum State Expansion Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state expansion algorithm based on self-adaptive topology, aiming to enhance the range of achievable quantum states and provide powerful tools for optimization and control within quantum computing. The core mechanism involves leveraging topological structure to dynamically expand the Hilbert space of quantum states, offering a pathway to more efficient quantum computations. Traditional approaches often rely on manual design, hindering the potential for automated learning and optimization. This work proposes a framework that automatically discovers and utilizes topological structures to expand the Hilbert space, offering a new paradigm for quantum state manipulation. The algorithm's potential impact lies in its ability to unlock new computational capabilities and facilitate the development of more sophisticated quantum algorithms.

title: Title: Algorithmic Consciousness with Contextual Bias
abstract: This paper explores the concept of algorithmic consciousness, aiming to develop an AI system capable of nuanced reasoning and adaptive behavior through a novel approach centered on contextual bias and cognitive weighting. We propose an algorithm that learns to subtly adjust its output based on observed user behavior and environmental context, thereby fostering a degree of 'understanding' – a critical step towards truly conscious AI. The core mechanism involves a dynamic cognitive weighting system that adjusts the algorithm's output based on observed data. This research addresses the challenge of moving beyond simple accuracy optimization, introducing a layer of adaptability and potential for genuine problem-solving. The focus is on establishing a framework for AI that can reason and respond intelligently to complex situations, ultimately pushing the boundaries of artificial intelligence.

title: 基于图的自适应机器学习的知识迁移
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for knowledge transfer utilizing graph-based self-adaptive machine learning. Traditional machine learning often relies on specific datasets, limiting its ability to generalize effectively. Our approach addresses this limitation by employing a graph-structured learning algorithm that dynamically adapts to the underlying graph structure and node relationships. We introduce a framework that automatically adjusts the learning process based on the graph's inherent characteristics, leading to enhanced knowledge transfer and improved generalization performance. The core mechanism centers around a self-adaptive learning algorithm that leverages graph structure and node relationships to establish a mapping of knowledge from one graph to another. The paper details the design of this framework, explores its implementation, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its performance through illustrative examples. The goal is to develop a robust and adaptable method for knowledge transfer, significantly enhancing the capabilities of machine learning models across diverse graph-based datasets.

title: Quantum Information Bottleneck Mitigation (QIBM)
abstract: Quantum information networks, crucial for advanced quantum computing and distributed quantum sensing, are plagued by the infamous information bottleneck. This bottleneck limits the speed and scalability of quantum communication and computation, hindering progress in these fields. This paper introduces the Quantum State Synchronization Protocol (QIBM), a novel system designed to effectively mitigate this bottleneck by minimizing the delay between quantum components. We detail the protocol's architecture, operational principles, and potential impact on network performance. The focus is on enhancing the robustness and efficiency of quantum information transfer, ultimately paving the way for more reliable and practical quantum technologies.

title: Probability Field Theory Under Non-linear Gradient Descent Optimization
abstract: Probability Field Theory (PFT) offers a novel approach to optimization by incorporating probabilistic elements into the optimization process. This paper investigates the application of PFT to gradient descent optimization, specifically focusing on mitigating the issues of gradient vanishing and exploding. We introduce a novel mechanism that leverages the probabilistic nature of the gradient field to enhance the optimization process, particularly when dealing with non-linear functions. This research explores the potential of PFT to improve the efficiency and robustness of gradient-based optimization algorithms. The core claim is that the introduction of probabilistic elements into the gradient descent framework can lead to more effective learning of complex functions, especially in scenarios involving non-linear functions.

title: 基于动态的拓扑变换的贝叶斯网络
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Bayesian network framework, termed "Dynamic Topological Transform Network" (DTT-Net), that leverages dynamic topology transformations as probabilistic models. The core mechanism centers on constructing a probability distribution representing the transformation process, enabling prediction and optimization using a Bayesian network. This approach addresses limitations of traditional Bayesian networks by incorporating a dynamic element, offering improved accuracy and adaptability in complex topology transformations. We present a practical implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of the DTT-Net in modeling and manipulating topological structures, highlighting its potential for advanced applications in fields requiring precise and flexible topology manipulation.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint Optimization for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum-enhanced constraint optimization to accelerate the training and improve generalization of neural networks. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the complexity of large neural networks, requiring significant computational resources and time. We propose a novel quantum algorithm, employing quantum annealing or quantum-enhanced gradient descent, to dynamically adjust the weights of the neural network. The core claim is that this approach can significantly reduce training time and improve the model's ability to generalize to unseen data. The paper details the theoretical framework, algorithm implementation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the potential benefits of this quantum-driven approach.

title: Nonlinear Topological Structures for Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Quantum algorithm optimization is a significant challenge in the field of quantum computing. Traditional optimization methods often focus on maximizing computational throughput, while the inherent complexity of quantum systems necessitates a novel approach. This paper introduces a novel framework, termed "Nonlinear Topological Structures for Quantum Algorithm Optimization," which leverages the unique properties of non-linear topological structures to guide the optimization process. The core mechanism involves mapping the quantum algorithm's parameters to a topological space, allowing for the exploration of diverse parameter configurations through a process of 'topological folding' and 'pathfinding.' We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of simulations and analysis, showcasing significant improvements in algorithm efficiency and stability compared to existing methods. The study highlights the potential of utilizing non-linear topology to address challenges in quantum algorithm design and optimization.

title: Self-Organizing Topological Quantum Computing Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computing algorithm based on self-organizing topological structures. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on precise parameter adjustments and complex control sequences, which can be computationally intensive and susceptible to errors. This research explores the potential of utilizing topological structures to enhance quantum computation by dynamically adjusting the quantum state to optimize performance. We detail a method for generating and manipulating these topological states, showcasing its ability to improve the fidelity of quantum operations and ultimately enhance the efficiency of quantum algorithms. The core of this work lies in a framework that leverages the inherent robustness and adaptability of topological phases to mitigate errors and accelerate computations. The algorithm's design incorporates a novel optimization strategy based on the topological properties of the generated states, leading to a demonstrable improvement in quantum state fidelity compared to existing approaches. This advancement holds significant promise for advancing the practical application of quantum computing.

title: Arnold's Bifurcation Principle Applied to Deployed Neural Networks: Real-Time Hardware Detection of Adversarial and Out-of-Distribution Inputs Using Hessian-Free Curvature-Velocity Tracking
abstract: A trained neural network, once put into service, is treated as fixed: its parameters do not change. What does change, continuously, is the stream of inputs it is asked to judge. Some of these inputs are ordinary. Some have been deliberately altered by an attacker to force a wrong answer. Some are simply unlike anything the network has ever seen. Earlier published work has already shown that both of these situations share a measurable signature: the local curvature of the network’s loss surface with respect to the input, which is the largest eigenvalue of the input-space Hessian, tends to be higher for adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs than for ordinary ones. Existing detection methods use this curvature as a single number, checked at one moment, against a fixed cutoff. We show that the same early-warning construction used throughout the Arnold’s Bifurcation Principle framework– tracking not the curvature itself but the phase-space pair formed by the curvature and its own rate of change– can be applied here as well, in a small piece of dedicated hardware sitting beside the main inference accelerator. We are explicit about a real cost difference from our earlier work on AI training: unlike a training run, where the required curvature information comes for free from steps the optimizer is already taking, an inference-time input stream does not always provide this for free, and we describe exactly when it does and when it requires a small added probe cost

title: Построение замкнутой программной среды в Unix-подобных операционных системах с использованием средств защиты пользовательского пространства
abstract: Целью работы является противодействие запуску недоверенного кода в Unix-подобных операционных системах. Объектом исследования является замкнутая программная среда. Задачи, решаемые в ходе исследования: 1. Исследовать механизм работы замкнутой программной среды в Unix-подобных операционных системах. 2. Исследовать возможности запуска недоверенного кода в замкнутой программной среде. 3. Предложить механизм защиты от запуска недоверенного кода в замкнутой программной среде. 4. Реализовать и провести тестирование предложенного механизма защиты. В ходе работы была исследована работа замкнутой программной среды и её реализация с помощью подсистем Linux IMA и veriexec. Была продемонстрирована возможность запуска недоверенного кода в замкнутой программной среде. В результате работы был разработан механизм пользовательского пространства, который позволяет предотвратить возможность запуска недоверенного кода. Данный механизм был реализован на практике и протестирован. Был сделан вывод о его эффективности в сравнении с другими механизмами. Полученные результаты могут быть использованы при проектирование замкнутой программной среды для обеспечения безопасности системы.

title: Task-Aware QUBO Allocation for Mixed-Precision Quantization
abstract: Mixed-precision quantization requires discrete allocation of weight and activation bit-widths, followed by recovery of the selected network. We develop a task-aware quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) surrogate with separate weight and activation profiles, a bit-operation (BOP) cost, and selected structural priors. QUBO provides a network-wide allocation that can be refined through direct validation-based PROTES search. On a compact NAFBlock-based denoiser, the refined route achieves 37.192 dB after LSQ+ at 4.035\% routed-layer BOPs, versus 37.092 dB at 4.101\% for a HAWQ-style baseline. The repeated-search primary experiment shows that LSQ+ largely closes the quality gap between QUBO allocation and expensive direct refinement. An additional restoration architecture retains a larger recovered gain, indicating that refinement's value depends on architecture and recovery. We evaluate quality, achieved cost, routing stability and optimization expense together. Deployment measurements characterize a fake-quantized floating-point implementation; BOP reductions describe analytical allocation savings.

title: Reflection-aware Generative Novel View Synthesis
abstract: We propose Ref-GeNVS, a training-free, reflection-aware method for generative novel view synthesis (NVS) in mirror scenes. Existing multi-view diffusion models often fail to recognize the mirror in the scene and cannot exploit reflected content for scene generation. To fix this issue without additional training, our key idea is to treat a mirror image as two complementary views. From input images, we estimate the mirror plane and reflect camera poses to form virtual views. Based on this virtual view setup, we propose a two-stage generation method consisting of Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection, which enables reflection-consistent NVS by explicitly leveraging reflection relationships in a multi-view diffusion model. Ref-GeNVS inherits the strong generalizability of the multi-view diffusion backbone, while it does not require finetuning. On synthetic and real scenes including mirrors, Ref-GeNVS outperforms recent generative NVS methods by generating reflection-consistent and contextually coherent novel views, revealing scene structure visible only through mirrors. Project page: https://kim-geonu.github.io/Ref-GeNVS/

title: LetOccVote: Learning Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy through Consensus
abstract: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction reduces the reliance on costly 3D annotations by learning from 2D pseudo-labels generated by vision foundation models. However, existing methods typically use these imperfect pseudo-labels directly as supervision, making occupancy learning vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets. We observe that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{LetOccVote}, a weakly supervised Gaussian-based occupancy framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve both geometric and semantic supervision. For geometry, Depth Vote exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision. For semantics, Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations. On Occ3D-nuScenes, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.

title: Label-Efficient 3D Point Cloud Understanding: From Representation Learning to Foundation Model Adaptation
abstract: Point clouds are the native output of modern 3D sensors that power autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality, yet their irregular, permutation-invariant, and geometrically rich structure - together with the high cost of 3D annotation - makes fully supervised learning impractical. In this thesis, we propose novel methods for label-efficient 3D perception that span from learning representations directly on raw point clouds to adapting pre-trained 3D foundation models under limited supervision and distribution shift. We first address representation learning by proposing CrossMoCo, a cross-modal momentum-contrastive framework that jointly pre-trains point cloud and image encoders to learn transferable representations. We further propose AllMatch that targets the limitation of pseudo-labelling in semi-supervised learning, so that every unlabelled sample - not only high-confidence ones - contributes, recovering near fully supervised accuracy with a small fraction of the labels. We next address adaptation by proposing MCFT, an adapter-free fine-tuning paradigm that curbs overfitting at no additional inference cost. We further propose ReFine3D that extends this idea to multi-modal 3D vision-language models, adding multi-view consistency and text-diversity regularization for robustness to novel classes, data corruptions, and cross-dataset shift. Finally, we propose SAGE by introducing an end-to-end, encoder-free 3D multi-modal large language model that resolves semantic misalignment and resolution mismatch challenges by treating point clouds as a foreign language. Together, these contributions advance robust, scalable 3D understanding toward practical, annotation-light deployment.

title: Explicitly correlated wavefunctions as classical seeds and property references for sample-based quantum diagonalization beyond the Born–Oppenheimer approximation
abstract: This work evaluates how well hybrid classical–quantum simulation methods capture not only the energy of small atomic and molecular systems, but also their other properties: contact densities, molecular structure, and state identity — the spin sector a computed state actually lives in. It employs explicitly correlated Gaussian (ECG) wavefunctions both as references for evaluating these properties and as classical seeds for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), on the simulator and on IBM quantum hardware. Our testbeds — positronium hydride, the muonic heliumlike ions, the HD+ molecular ion, and the positronium anion and molecule — realize three typical failure regimes: boxes that lack the property no matter how configurations are selected, boxes that hold it exactly with no selection needed, and the middle regime where the selection itself decides. In every regime the property error dwarfs the energy error: a subspace can converge the energy to microhartrees while misstating an annihilation rate, a bond length, or the spin by whole percent. Property fidelity, not energy, is the discriminating test of a multicomponent simulation.

title: Geometric Complexity of Stochastic Processes via Bayesian Filtering
abstract: This paper investigates the geometric complexity of stochastic processes, focusing on high-dimensional scenarios. We propose a Bayesian filtering framework, termed "Geometric Bayesian Estimation," designed to quantify complexity more effectively than traditional methods. The core mechanism involves exploiting geometric properties inherent to the process to refine estimates of its dimensionality and structure. This approach aims to address limitations in existing Bayesian techniques, particularly concerning the analysis of high-dimensional data. The paper details the algorithm, its theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy.

title: Title: Non-Linear Harmonic Field Dynamics with Adaptive Amplitude Scaling
abstract: This paper investigates the modeling and simulation of non-linear harmonic field dynamics, focusing on a novel algorithm leveraging reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust field amplitude based on the system's internal state. Traditional harmonic field simulations frequently rely on fixed parameters, restricting their applicability to specific system configurations. We propose a new approach that utilizes a reinforcement learning framework to train a neural network to optimize field amplitude in real-time, providing enhanced flexibility and adaptability. The algorithm addresses the limitations of current simulation techniques by enabling the system to self-regulate its field characteristics. This work explores the potential for this approach to unlock new functionalities and applications in diverse fields, including materials science, fluid dynamics, and sensor systems. The core mechanism centers on a reinforcement learning agent trained to respond to a system's internal state, dynamically adjusting the amplitude of the field.

title: Title: Adaptive Cognitive Geometry (ACG)
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Cognitive Geometry (ACG), a novel computational framework for generating and evolving cognitive geometry. The core claim is that ACG can dynamically shape the structure of a space based on an individual's internal cognitive processes and understanding of the world. The system employs neural network-inspired algorithms to 'learn' the geometry of space, creating a personalized geometric representation. This research explores the potential of leveraging cognitive processes within a computational model, offering a potential paradigm shift in how we understand and model the relationship between mind and perception. The paper details the architecture of the ACG system, including the neural network components and the process of generating and evolving the geometric representation. We discuss the potential applications and limitations of this approach, focusing on its ability to capture and model complex cognitive processes.

title: Title: Non-Local Wave Function Collapse for Parallel Quantum Computation
abstract: Abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum computation, termed Non-Local Wave Function Collapse (NLWC), designed to accelerate quantum algorithms through simultaneous wave function collapse across multiple processors. Traditional quantum algorithms often face scalability challenges, necessitating efficient methods for handling complex quantum states. NLWC proposes a mechanism that drastically reduces computation time by allowing the collapse of multiple states concurrently, offering a potential pathway to exponential speedups in specific quantum algorithms. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments. The core mechanism leverages a dynamic state mapping that facilitates rapid collapse across a large state space, significantly reducing the time required to evaluate quantum circuits. This research contributes to a fundamental understanding of parallel quantum computation and offers a promising framework for achieving substantial speedups in various quantum applications.

title: 基于自适应量子势的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive quantum potentials, designed to address the challenges of optimizing complex models effectively. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their applicability to diverse model structures. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts the quantum potential during the optimization process, adapting to the model's inherent complexity. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing optimization techniques across multiple benchmark datasets. The core mechanism leverages a novel approach to model parameter adjustment based on a dynamically evolving quantum potential, offering enhanced precision and adaptability within complex optimization scenarios.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry: A Quantum Entanglement-Based Computational Model
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-linear topological geometry, leveraging quantum entanglement, to provide a novel computational model for precise geometric simulation. The core claim is the design of a computational framework that harnesses the unique properties of quantum entanglement to accelerate complex geometric computations and mitigate the inherent errors associated with traditional methods. The proposed mechanism involves incorporating quantum entanglement within the core computation process, offering a pathway to achieve accurate results with enhanced computational efficiency. This work introduces a new approach to topological geometry computation, potentially revolutionizing the field by offering a fundamentally different methodology.

title: Quantum Entangled State Transfer Optimization – An Extended Topological Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Entangled State Transfer (QEST) represents a paradigm shift in secure communication, moving beyond traditional encryption methods and leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. This paper explores the optimization of QEST using a novel hybrid approach that integrates quantum state adaptation and topological optimization. We propose a system where the quantum state is dynamically transformed through a tailored topological algorithm, enhancing information protection and ultimately boosting transfer efficiency. The core mechanism centers around the strategic application of a topological transformation to quantum states, yielding significant improvements in the fidelity and speed of transfer. This work presents a framework for significantly enhancing the capabilities of QEST, pushing the boundaries of secure communication through the synergistic integration of quantum entanglement and topological optimization. The paper details the methodology, results, and preliminary analysis of this new approach.

title: 混沌理论的量子化计算框架
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computation framework leveraging the unique properties of chaos. Traditional quantum computation often focuses on the underlying quantum algorithms, while chaos theory offers a powerful tool for understanding and optimizing computational processes. We propose a quantum algorithm designed to transform the quantum computation itself into a quantum chaotic system, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. This framework utilizes the inherent self-organization of chaos to achieve significant improvements in algorithm performance. The core mechanism involves mapping the core quantum computation to the dynamics of a chaotic system, effectively amplifying the system's response to perturbations and promoting faster convergence to a stable solution. This work explores the potential of this approach to unlock new capabilities in quantum computation, addressing limitations currently faced by existing algorithms.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Temporal Graph Kernels
abstract: Anomaly detection in graph-structured data is a crucial task across diverse domains, including social network analysis, fraud detection, and cybersecurity. Traditional graph anomaly detection methods often struggle to effectively capture the dynamic nature of graphs, which evolve over time. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing temporal graph kernels to address this limitation. The core idea is to define kernels that measure the similarity between graph structures at different points in time, allowing for the detection of anomalous changes in graph connectivity and node behavior. The proposed method leverages the power of kernel methods to efficiently compute these temporal similarities, providing a robust and scalable solution for anomaly detection in evolving graph environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential with a conceptual framework, highlighting its applicability to various real-world scenarios. The key contribution lies in the systematic development and application of temporal graph kernels, representing a significant advancement in graph anomaly detection techniques.

title: 基于动态拓扑的量子机器学习框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning framework based on dynamic topology, leveraging the unique properties of quantum systems to perform complex machine learning tasks. We propose a method where the input to the quantum algorithm is dynamically constructed from a set of topological structures, and a dynamic topology optimization algorithm is employed to tailor the learning process. The core mechanism of this framework centers on the integration of dynamic topology into the quantum computation process, aiming to achieve efficient and effective quantum machine learning. The work presents a preliminary demonstration of this framework's capabilities through specific examples, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of existing quantum machine learning approaches.

title: Quantum Entanglement Non-Asymmetry Theory
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, remains a profoundly mysterious phenomenon. While its existence has been experimentally verified, its fundamental nature remains largely inaccessible to direct manipulation. This paper presents a novel theoretical framework, "Non-Asymmetric Entanglement Theory" (NAET), designed to address this challenge. NAET proposes a fundamentally new approach to understanding and utilizing entanglement by explicitly incorporating non-symmetry into its core principles. We explore the implications of this integration for quantum computation, focusing on enhancing entanglement strength and stability. The theoretical model developed leverages a carefully constructed concept of "Non-Asymmetric Entanglement" to provide a new perspective on the limitations and potential of current quantum algorithms. This work aims to provide a more comprehensive and mathematically rigorous understanding of entanglement, offering a pathway to enhanced quantum computing capabilities.

title: Dynamic Probability Distribution Evolutionary Algorithm: Adaptive Feature Selection Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel evolutionary algorithm based on dynamically adjusted probability distributions, designed for rapid optimization of complex problems. The core mechanism involves a continuous, adaptive feature selection process, driven by the algorithm's internal probability distribution. This approach distinguishes the algorithm from traditional evolutionary methods by its inherent flexibility and capacity to respond to evolving data characteristics. The paper details the design of the dynamic probability distribution, the optimization process, and the resulting performance improvements in a series of benchmark datasets. We demonstrate that the adaptive feature selection strategy consistently outperforms static feature selection methods across a range of problem types. The algorithm's efficiency stems from its ability to iteratively refine feature representations based on observed data, ultimately leading to more robust and accurate solutions.

title: Memory Network Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning algorithm, Memory Network Reinforcement Learning (MNERL), designed to enhance learning efficiency and generalization capabilities by leveraging a memory matrix. Traditional reinforcement learning struggles with long-term dependencies, and our approach introduces a "memory matrix" to efficiently store and retrieve past experience. The algorithm utilizes this matrix to accelerate learning and improve the model's ability to generalize to unseen scenarios. We present a rigorous analysis of the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in complex environments.

abstract: This paper presents a novel system optimization algorithm based on dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). Traditional optimization methods often require manual parameter adjustment, limiting their applicability to complex scenarios. This work introduces a dynamic Bayesian network-based approach that automatically adjusts model parameters and optimizes the system model, resulting in improved system performance. The core mechanism leverages the dynamic nature of the DBN to iteratively refine the model based on feedback and constraints, leading to a more robust and adaptive optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of simulations and comparisons with existing optimization techniques.
